terms.gloss: turn everything upside down, throw everything into confusion
evidence: Sall. Cat. 10.1: saevīre fortūna ac miscēre omnia coepit (Lewis & Short s.v. saeviō)
terms.comment: Miscēre, to mix, is also to throw into disorder; in the passive, omnia mixta.

evidence: Sen. Ep. 44.4: omnia ista sūrsum deorsum fortūna versāvit, fortune has turned all that topsy-turvy (Lewis & Short s.v. sūrsum, “prov.”)
Petr. 65: quod sūrsum est, deorsum faciunt, they turn everything upside down (Lewis & Short s.v. sūrsum)
terms.comment: Of movement the pair means “up and down, to and fro” (see up and down); with a verb of turning it is “topsy-turvy”, as in Seneca. Traupman’s omnia sūrsum deorsum versāre is Seneca’s phrase; for omnia erant sūrsum deorsum, with no verb of turning, we have found no classical instance.

sources: Quotations marked “Lewis & Short” are given as Lewis & Short cites them, in the house spelling; they have not been checked against a modern edition.
John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, p. 110.
